description: I build evidence-first geospatial software. TerraTrace compares terrain morphology across Earth, Mars, the Moon, Mercury and Ceres at a common spatial support, decides by Pareto dominance instead of a single score, and refuses to claim traversability, site access or geologic equivalence — it can return TIE or INDETERMINATE. 843 offline tests, 51 scientific oracles, and a benchmark that once made us withdraw our own finding.
summary: TerraTrace is a reproducible terrain-morphology screening engine built for the challenge Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars. It compares real planetary elevation data — NASA MOLA for Mars, LRO LOLA for the Moon, Copernicus GLO-30 for Earth — on an exact common metric grid at a declared support, then answers three questions separately: which candidate is least dissimilar (Pareto dominance, never a composite score), whether any candidate lies inside the reference’s own variability, and whether the evidence is strong enough to say either. It refuses when it is not: a comparison that cannot be made at the same scale is blocked, and a variability band that admits terrain known to be different is demoted rather than reported as a match. Its most important result is a claim it disproved about itself — an earlier Mars analog it withdrew under a protocol frozen before the data — followed by a measurement of why. Every number is reproducible from committed code with no API key, and the engine contains no model, no network call and no runtime inference.
details:
What it does. TerraTrace ingests planetary elevation data, reprojects each area of interest onto its own local azimuthal-equidistant metric grid using the correct body radius (Mars 3,396,190 m; Moon 1,737,400 m; Mercury 2,439,400 m; Ceres 469,730 m; Earth WGS84), and computes map-scale descriptors — slope, local relief, detrended ruggedness, connectivity, aspect dispersion, hypsometric integral, and a 40-family descriptor bank of roughly 290 scalar values. It then compares a reference terrain against Earth candidates by Pareto dominance and reports three separable verdicts.

How it works. Declared config → fail-fast preflight (no network; it validates bounds and sizes the request) → source catalog selection → fetch (NASA MOLA and Copernicus GLO-30 are both keyless) → per-body metric grid → masking and quality gates (water, sentinel, flat-run, valid fraction) → descriptor bank → comparability gate → Pareto decision → three verdicts → a hashed, provenance-tracked artifact package → viewer, site, decks and paper.

Why it is important. A false analog is expensive to build on. The contribution is not a postcard of a lookalike terrain but a method that detects its own false analogs: it withdrew a previously published Mars analog under a protocol frozen before the data, measured the explanation (the nearest Earth analog tracks kilometre-scale roughness, not volcanic origin), and publishes the bound on its own headline. On the lunar panel it reports the ranking and the adequacy question separately, refuses to call the leading candidate adequate, and states what cannot transfer — no traversability, hazard, geological equivalence, site access or mission-readiness claim.

Tools and languages. Python with NumPy for the engine (dependency-free test runner, 1044 tests, 51 analytic validation oracles); rasterio/GDAL, pyproj and PROJ for the optional GIS paths; a dependency-free SVG/HTML generator for the figures and the offline evidence atlas; vanilla HTML/CSS/JS for the published site; Node with pptxgenjs for the slide generators.

Creativity and factors considered. Three separate answers instead of one score, so a ranking can never be mistaken for an adequacy result; a comparability gate that can block rather than force a comparison; an adequacy band calibrated from the reference’s own held-out variability, and demoted when it admits known-different terrain; and a reproducibility discipline in which every published number is regenerated and checked by a documentation guard that fails the build when prose drifts from the code. We deliberately excluded Mars from the lunar comparison rather than forcing a source below its own resolution.
